981.title: the Bhagavata's tenth book continued
981.hook: with Kamsa gone, Krishna goes to school, and the teacher's fee is a boy the ocean took
981.carry: going as far as it takes
981.howItsDone: Hindus honor teachers on Guru Purnima, and the custom of guru dakshina, a gift to a teacher at the end of study, continues in some traditional music, dance and scriptural schools; Krishna's fee to Sandipani is one story told when people speak of what a student owes a teacher.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Gita Govinda at its front door: bhakti as smarana, remembering, again and again, and your line, let the beloved come back to mind. Who came back to mind at the red light? Day nine hundred eighty-one.
screen: `BHAKTI.` · `SMARANA: REMEMBERING.`

segments.voice: Kamsa is dead. His father Ugrasena is back on the throne of Mathura. Vasudeva and Devaki have their sons again. So what does the hero of the story do next? He goes to school. The Bhagavata's tenth book picks up the thread here, right after the arena, and sends Krishna and his brother Balarama off to study with a teacher in the city of Avanti, a brahmin named Sandipani. They sit at his feet like any other students. And at the end, when it's time to pay, the teacher asks for something no student could give.
screen: `KAMSA IS GONE.` → `THE HERO GOES TO SCHOOL.` → `A FEE NO STUDENT COULD PAY.`

segments.voice: First, the strangeness of it. In the Bhagavata, Krishna is the Lord himself. Why would he need a teacher? The text's own answer, in paraphrase, is that the two brothers, though they were the source of all knowledge, chose to live in a teacher's house to show the world how it's done. They serve Sandipani, and they learn fast: the Vedas, the sciences, the use of weapons, the arts. Then comes the fee, the guru dakshina, the gift a student gives a teacher when the studies end. Sandipani talks it over with his wife. And they ask for the one thing they can't stop grieving: their son, who was lost in the ocean at Prabhasa. Not gold. Their boy. So Krishna and Balarama go to the shore. The ocean tells them a demon living in the shape of a conch, Panchajana, took the child. Krishna goes into the water, overcomes him, and takes the conch shell. The boy isn't there. So Krishna goes all the way to the city of Yama, the lord of death, and blows that conch at the gate. Yama comes out, honors him, and gives the child back. And the brothers walk home and hand their teacher his son. Two things are worth keeping. One is the order of loyalties. Before anything else in his new life, Krishna honors a teacher. The other is the size of the gift. A guru dakshina, in this story, isn't a payment that settles the account. It's the student going as far as it takes. And that conch, Panchajanya, doesn't leave the story. On the battlefield at the start of the Gita, it's the conch Krishna blows.
screen: `WHY WOULD THE LORD NEED A TEACHER?` · `THE FEE: OUR LOST SON.` · `A CONCH AT YAMA'S GATE.` · `THE STUDENT GOES AS FAR AS IT TAKES.` · then, large: `GURU DAKSHINA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one teacher who changed something for you. A schoolteacher, a grandparent, a coach, someone at work. Picture the room where they taught you, and one thing they said there. Then ask, quietly: what would I give them, if I could? Don't worry about whether it's possible. Just let the answer come. If you pray, you can hold that teacher in your prayer. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with thanks. The bell holds the time.
Guru dakshina. The gift a student gives a teacher when the studies end. Today, Krishna as a student, and a teacher's fee paid at the gate of death.
screen: `GURU DAKSHINA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: going as far as it takes. Today, thank one teacher, out loud or in a short note, for one specific thing. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

982.title: the Bhagavata's tenth book continued
982.hook: a learned friend arrives in Vraja at sunset, and a father asks him one question all night
982.howItsDone: In Vaishnava traditions, the chapters of Uddhava's visit to Vraja are read aloud in Bhagavata recitations and sung in devotional songs, and Nanda and Yashoda are honored as models of parental love for Krishna.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhagavata's tenth book went on: Krishna at school, and a teacher's fee paid at the gate of death, going as far as it takes. Which teacher did you thank? Day nine hundred eighty-two.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `GURU DAKSHINA.`

segments.voice: In Mathura, Krishna calls his friend and counselor Uddhava aside. Go to Vraja, he tells him. Comfort my father and mother. Comfort the gopis. Tell them what I've told you. So Uddhava drives out to the village Krishna grew up in. He arrives at sunset. The cows are coming home, raising dust. Calves are calling. There's the sound of milking, lamps being lit, butter being churned. It's an ordinary evening in a place that has been missing someone for a long time. And the first person to meet him is Nanda, Krishna's foster father.
screen: `GO TO VRAJA. COMFORT THEM.` → `SUNSET. COWS COMING HOME.` → `NANDA MEETS HIM AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Nanda embraces Uddhava as if he were Krishna himself, washes his feet, feeds him, and sits him down. Then come the questions, in paraphrase. Is he well? Does Krishna remember us? His mother, his friends, the cows, the forest, the hill he held up? Will he come back, even once, so we can see his face? And then Nanda starts remembering out loud: the forest fire, the serpent in the river, the storm. He can't finish. His voice breaks. Beside him, Yashoda, his mother, is listening to every word, and the text says her tears won't stop. Uddhava answers as a learned man would. You two are truly fortunate, he says, to love him like this. And then he says something large. Krishna isn't only your son. He has no mother or father of his own, no one who is his and no one who isn't. He is within everyone, the Self of all beings. Will that help a mother whose tears won't stop? The Bhagavata doesn't pretend it settles anything. It just lets them talk, the father and the counselor, through the whole night. And here's the quiet thing the scene does. It puts a vast teaching, Krishna as the Self of all, right next to a small, human grief: does he remember us? It doesn't choose between them. Both are true in that room. Then morning comes. The women of Vraja are up, churning butter, and as they churn they sing about Krishna, and the song carries out over the village. Life goes on in Vraja. It goes on full of him.
screen: `DOES HE REMEMBER US?` · `NANDA REMEMBERS, AND BREAKS.` · `HE IS THE SELF OF ALL.` · `THE BIG TRUTH AND THE SMALL GRIEF.` · then, large: `AT DAWN, THEY CHURN AND SING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the body be heavy on the chair. Bring to mind a household that is missing someone: your own, or one you know. Don't look for the right words for it. Just let yourself sit in that house for a minute, the way Uddhava sat with Nanda, listening. Breathe in. Breathe out. If you pray, you can hold that household in your prayer. If you don't, simply keep them company in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Uddhava, Krishna's trusted friend and counselor, sent to comfort the family he left behind. Today, a father who asks if he's remembered, and a mother whose tears won't stop.
screen: `UDDHAVA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: does he remember us. Today, ask someone who's missing a person about them, and then mostly listen. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

983.title: the Bhagavata's tenth book continued
983.hook: an army arrives at the gate, and Krishna walks out alone, unarmed, and starts to run
983.carry: he ran, and he chose where to run
983.howItsDone: In parts of Gujarat, Krishna is worshipped as Ranchhod or Ranchhodrai, the one who left the battlefield, and devotees tell the story of the chase to Muchukunda's cave as part of that name's meaning.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhagavata's tenth book continued back in Vraja: Uddhava and Nanda, talking all night, and a father asking, does he remember us? Who did you listen to? Day nine hundred eighty-three.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `DOES HE REMEMBER US?`

segments.voice: Mathura has no peace. Jarasandha, the powerful king whose daughters were married to Kamsa, attacks the city again and again. Krishna turns his armies back each time, and each time Jarasandha returns. Now a second enemy is marching on the city as well, a fierce king called Kalayavana, with a vast army. Two forces, one city. And here the Bhagavata gives its hero a strange move. Krishna walks out through the city gate, alone, without a weapon, wearing a garland, and lets the enemy king see him. Then he turns and runs.
screen: `JARASANDHA, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `KALAYAVANA AT THE GATE.` → `KRISHNA WALKS OUT, AND RUNS.`

segments.voice: First, he protects his people. Before he steps outside, Krishna has a new city built in the sea, Dwaraka, and the text says he moves the people of Mathura there by his own power, so they wake up somewhere safe. Only then does he walk out to meet Kalayavana. The king recognizes him from what he's heard: the dark one, the lotus eyes, the garland. And, being a proud man, he decides to chase him on foot, without weapons, man to man. Krishna stays just out of reach. Across the open ground, up into the hills, and into a mountain cave. Kalayavana charges in after him, into the dark, and sees a man lying asleep. He thinks it's Krishna, pretending. So he kicks him. The sleeper is Muchukunda, an ancient king who once fought for the gods and asked them, as his reward, for sleep. He wakes, he looks at the man who kicked him, and the text says that at his glance Kalayavana burns to ashes. Then Krishna steps out of the shadows and shows himself to the old king. Muchukunda is overwhelmed. He praises him at length, and when Krishna offers him a boon, he asks for nothing but devotion. So who won? Krishna never lifted a weapon. He ran, and he chose where to run. Tradition in Gujarat gives him a name for this, Ranchhod, which devotees explain as the one who left the battlefield. It's not an insult there. It's a title of love. In this chapter, the Bhagavata's tenth book shows a hero who protects his people first, isn't too proud to run, and lets the right moment do the work.
screen: `FIRST, A CITY IN THE SEA.` · `THE CHASE INTO THE CAVE.` · `THE SLEEPER WAKES: MUCHUKUNDA.` · `RANCHHOD: THE ONE WHO LEFT THE FIELD.` · then, large: `HE NEVER LIFTED A WEAPON.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one fight you're in right now. At work, at home, in your own head. Ask it the question this chapter raises, gently: does this need to be won today, here, on this ground? Or can I step back, and let a better moment come? Don't decide anything yet. Just let the question sit. If you pray, you can bring that fight into your prayer. If you don't, simply breathe, and let it rest for now. The bell holds the time.
Ranchhod, explained by devotees as the one who left the battlefield, a loving name for Krishna in Gujarat. Today, the city built in the sea, and the chase into Muchukunda's cave.
screen: `RANCHHOD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: he ran, and he chose where to run. Today, walk away from one argument that doesn't need winning, and notice how that feels. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

984.title: the Bhagavata's tenth book continued
984.hook: a princess is about to be married to the wrong man, so she writes a letter and finds someone to carry it
984.carry: I have heard, and I have chosen
984.howItsDone: Rukmini is worshipped beside Krishna in temples, and some Hindus recite her letter from the Bhagavata, especially when praying for a good marriage; the story is also staged in dance and drama.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhagavata's tenth book continued with a chase: Krishna running unarmed into Muchukunda's cave, and the name Ranchhod, he ran, and he chose where to run. Which argument did you walk away from? Day nine hundred eighty-four.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `RANCHHOD.`

segments.voice: A letter is traveling by road from the kingdom of Vidarbha to the city of Dwaraka. The man carrying it is an old brahmin, trusted, sworn to deliver it into one pair of hands. The woman who wrote it is the king's daughter, Rukmini. Her brother has arranged her marriage to a king she doesn't want: Shishupala, the man we met earlier this year at Yudhishthira's great rite. The wedding is coming. Her family has decided. And Rukmini has decided too, quietly, on her own. Today, what she wrote.
screen: `A LETTER ON THE ROAD TO DWARAKA.` → `A WEDDING SHE DIDN'T CHOOSE.` → `RUKMINI HAS DECIDED.`

segments.voice: In Dwaraka, Krishna receives the brahmin, washes his feet, feeds him, and only then asks why he's come. The brahmin hands him the letter, and the Bhagavata lets us read it, in paraphrase. I have heard of your qualities, Rukmini writes, and hearing them, my mind has gone to you and won't come back, and I've set shame aside. I have chosen you. Come and take my hand. Don't let the king of Chedi take what is yours, like a jackal stealing a lion's share. Then she does something practical. She gives him a plan. Come to Vidarbha before the wedding, unseen, with your forces. And she knows her own family's customs: before the wedding, the bride walks out of the city to the temple of the goddess Ambika. That's where you'll find me. And if you don't come, she says, I'll give up my life, and keep hoping for you life after life. Look at what kind of devotion this is. Rukmini has never seen Krishna. She has only heard about him. Prahlada's list of the ways of devotion, which we met a few days ago, begins with hearing. But she doesn't stop at longing. She writes, she plans, she risks. And Krishna answers right away: he gets into his chariot that same night. On the appointed day, Rukmini goes to the goddess's temple and prays. She walks out, and he's there. He lifts her into his chariot in front of everyone. There's a fight, and her brother chases them, and loses. In Dwaraka, they marry. Some devotees hear Rukmini as a picture of the soul that has heard of God, chosen God, and taken the first step.
screen: `I HAVE HEARD, AND I HAVE CHOSEN.` · `A PLAN: THE GODDESS'S TEMPLE.` · `SHE NEVER SAW HIM. SHE HEARD.` · `HE COMES THAT SAME NIGHT.` · then, large: `COME AND TAKE MY HAND.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath be easy. Rukmini's devotion started with hearing. So, for this sit, simply listen. Notice every sound you can: the far ones, the near ones, the sound of your own breath. Don't name them or judge them. Just receive them, one by one. If you pray, you can let a name you love be the sound you return to. If you don't, return to the breath whenever the mind wanders. The bell holds the time.
Rukmini, the princess of Vidarbha who became Krishna's queen. Today, her letter: devotion that begins by hearing, and then writes, plans and acts.
screen: `RUKMINI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I have heard, and I have chosen. Today, take one first step toward something you've chosen in your heart: send the message, make the call. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

985.title: the Bhagavata's tenth book continued
985.hook: a jewel goes missing, a rumor says Krishna took it, and he goes into the forest to find the truth
985.howItsDone: The Syamantaka story is told in Bhagavata recitations, and in some regions it is read or heard on Ganesh Chaturthi, as a story about false accusation and how it is cleared.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhagavata's tenth book continued with Rukmini's letter: I have heard, and I have chosen. What first step did you take? Day nine hundred eighty-five.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `I HAVE HEARD. I HAVE CHOSEN.`

segments.voice: Someone is walking toward Dwaraka so bright that the people in the streets shield their eyes. They run to Krishna: the sun god himself is coming to see you! Krishna laughs. It isn't the sun, he tells them. It's Satrajit, wearing his jewel. The jewel is the Syamantaka, a gift to Satrajit from the sun, and it's beautiful, and it brings wealth to whoever keeps it. Before long, it will go missing. And the city will start whispering a name. Krishna's.
screen: `IS THE SUN COMING?` → `NO: SATRAJIT AND HIS JEWEL.` → `THE CITY WHISPERS A NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's how it goes wrong, in paraphrase. Krishna asks Satrajit to give the jewel to the king, Ugrasena. Satrajit refuses. Not long after, Satrajit's brother Prasena wears it out hunting, and doesn't come back. A lion kills him and takes the jewel. Then a bear kills the lion and carries the jewel to his cave. But nobody in Dwaraka knows any of that. All they know is that Krishna wanted the jewel, and now the jewel and the man wearing it are gone. So people talk. Watch what Krishna does with that. He doesn't argue. He doesn't make a speech about his innocence. He goes and finds out. He takes some of the townspeople with him, and they follow the trail: Prasena's body, then the lion's, then the tracks of a bear, leading to a dark cave. Krishna goes in alone. The bear is Jambavan, the bear king who served Rama in the Ramayana. They fight in the dark, and it goes on and on. Finally, Jambavan understands who he's fighting: his own Lord, Rama, come again. He bows. Krishna explains he only came for the jewel, to clear his name. Jambavan gives it gladly, and his daughter Jambavati in marriage too. Back in Dwaraka, Krishna calls Satrajit before the whole assembly, hands him the jewel, and tells the full story in public. Satrajit is ashamed. He offers Krishna his daughter, Satyabhama, and the jewel as well. Krishna marries Satyabhama. The jewel, he gives back. He never wanted it. He wanted the truth told in front of the people who had heard the rumor.
screen: `THE JEWEL GOES MISSING.` · `HE DOESN'T ARGUE. HE FINDS OUT.` · `JAMBAVAN KNOWS HIS LORD.` · `THE TRUTH TOLD IN PUBLIC.` · then, large: `HE GIVES THE JEWEL BACK.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle low in the belly. Bring to mind one time someone believed something untrue about you. Notice what rises: heat, the urge to explain, maybe an old hurt. Don't push it away, and don't feed it. Just breathe with it, the way you'd sit with someone who's upset. If you pray, you can bring that hurt into your prayer. If you don't, simply let the breath be slower than the feeling. The bell holds the time.
Syamantaka, the jewel the sun gave Satrajit, and the rumor it caused in Dwaraka. Today, Krishna goes to find the truth instead of arguing his innocence.

986.hook: a poor man visits his richest friend, forgets to ask for anything, and walks home happy anyway
986.carry: a handful of rice, eaten with delight
986.howItsDone: Hindus tell the story of Sudama, also called Kuchela in South India, as a picture of friendship with God, and in some places devotees offer flattened rice to Krishna in memory of it.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhagavata's tenth book continued with the Syamantaka jewel: a rumor, a trail into the forest, and the truth told in public: he gives the jewel back. Did you check something before repeating it? Day nine hundred eighty-six.
screen: `THE TENTH BOOK, CONTINUED.` · `HE GIVES THE JEWEL BACK.`

segments.voice: A thin man in a torn cloth is standing at the gates of Dwaraka, holding a small bundle. He's a brahmin, poor enough that his family often goes hungry. His wife has sent him. Go to your old friend, she said. The one you studied with as a boy. He's the lord of Dwaraka now. Surely he'll help. The man didn't want to ask. He came mostly to see his friend's face. And in the bundle is the only gift his house could find: a few handfuls of flattened rice, begged from the neighbors. Tradition calls him Sudama.
screen: `A POOR MAN AT THE GATES.` → `GO TO YOUR OLD FRIEND.` → `A BUNDLE OF FLATTENED RICE.`

segments.voice: Krishna sees him from across the palace and gets up from where he's sitting with Rukmini, runs to him, and embraces him. He washes his friend's feet. Rukmini herself fans him. And the two old classmates talk about school, about Sandipani's house, the teacher we met earlier this week. Krishna reminds him of a night when the teacher's wife sent them for firewood, a storm caught them in the forest, and they held hands in the dark until their teacher came looking at dawn and blessed them. Then Krishna asks, smiling: what did you bring me? The brahmin is too ashamed to show it. So Krishna takes the bundle himself, opens it, and eats a handful of the rice with delight. As he reaches for more, Rukmini gently catches his hand, as if to say: that's enough. That one handful is plenty for everything your friend will ever need. The brahmin stays the night, and in the morning he walks home. He never asked. Krishna never offered. And he walks home happy, thinking, in paraphrase: he didn't give me wealth so that I wouldn't become proud and forget him. Then he reaches his village, and can't find his hut. In its place is a house shining like a palace, and his wife comes out to meet him. The Bhagavata gives him a last reflection: Krishna gives a great deal and counts it as little, and takes a small thing from his devotee and counts it as a great deal. The brahmin lives on in that house, and the text says he keeps his heart where it was. On Krishna.
screen: `KRISHNA RUNS TO HIM.` · `THE NIGHT IN THE STORM, AT SCHOOL.` · `ONE HANDFUL IS ENOUGH.` · `HE NEVER ASKED.` · then, large: `GIVES MUCH, COUNTS IT LITTLE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Let your eyes move slowly around the room and rest on one ordinary thing you already have: a cup, a blanket, a window, a pair of shoes. Stay with it. Notice who made it, or gave it, or what it has carried you through. The brahmin walked home glad before he knew what was waiting there. Let some of that gladness rest on this one small thing. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, simply let it be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
Sudama, the poor brahmin and Krishna's boyhood friend. Today, his flattened rice, and a friend who counts a small gift as a great one.

987.howItsDone: At a kirtan a leader often sings a line and the group sings it back, with harmonium, drum and hand cymbals; some groups open the evening with a song to Ganesha, who is honored before beginnings.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: This week we followed the Bhagavata's tenth book past the cowherd years: a teacher's fee, a princess's letter, a missing jewel, and yesterday a poor friend who never asked, a handful of rice, eaten with delight. Which scene would you tell first? Today the stories turn into songs. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.
screen: `THE BHAGAVATA'S TENTH BOOK.` · `PAST THE COWHERD YEARS.` · `NOW, THE SONGS.`

segments.voice: A rug on the floor, a harmonium in the middle of it, a pair of small hand cymbals waiting beside a drum. People drift in and sit cross-legged. Some know every word. Some have never been to a kirtan before and are already worried about singing badly. The leader presses a key, the drone begins, and before any song to Krishna or Shiva, the first line goes out to someone else. An elephant-headed god, with a broken tusk and a sweet in one hand. The room sings it back. Why start there?
screen: `A RUG, A HARMONIUM, A DRUM.` → `THE DRONE BEGINS.` → `THE FIRST SONG GOES TO GANESHA.`

segments.voice: Kirtan is singing the names and glories of God together, often as call and response. The leader sings a line, the room sings it back. A repertoire is simply the songs a group knows by heart, the ones that can start without a songbook. For the next few days we'll build one, a song at a time, in roughly the order an evening might run. Some halls begin with Ganesha. Tradition honors him first before many beginnings: a wedding, a new house, a school year, a puja. He is called the remover of obstacles, and also the lord of them, the one who can place a block in the road or lift it. Tradition tells more than one story of why he goes first. In one, from the Shiva Purana, Shiva restores the boy to life with an elephant's head after a terrible quarrel, and then declares that he will be worshipped before every other god. A Hindi aarti to him begins: Jai Ganesha, Jai Ganesha, Jai Ganesha Deva. Victory to Ganesha, victory to the god. The next line names his family plainly: his mother is Parvati, his father is Mahadeva, the great god, Shiva. So the first song of the night is partly a family introduction. Notice what that does in the room. This evening doesn't begin with the hardest song. It begins by clearing the road. The nervous newcomer gets a simple line to repeat, sung slowly, and by the third time round, the line is in the room. In a kirtan, the first obstacle can be as small as opening your mouth.
screen: `KIRTAN: NAMES SUNG BACK AND FORTH.` · `A REPERTOIRE: SONGS KNOWN BY HEART.` · `GANESHA, HONORED FIRST.` · `HIS SONG CLEARS THE ROAD.` · then, large: `BEGIN BY CLEARING THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the shoulders drop. Bring to mind one thing you're about to begin, today or this week. A conversation, a piece of work, a trip. Name it quietly. Then name one thing that might block it: tiredness, worry, a person, a habit. Don't try to solve it. Just see the obstacle clearly and set it down in front of you. If you pray, you can say Ganesha's name once, softly, as some Hindus do before a beginning. If not, simply rest with the road in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. The songs a group sings together by heart. Today, the song that often opens the night: Ganesha's.
